Season 1 of 'Elite Force' spent four weeks in Netflix’s global Top 10 for non-English-language shows.

Netflix has kicked off production on the second season of “Elite Force,” its hit French action thriller starring Tomer Sisley (“Largo Winch”).

Created by Julien Leclercq and Sylvain Caron and directed by Leclercq, the series spent four weeks in Netflix’s global Top 10 for non-English-language shows and cracked the streamer’s Top 10 in 91 countries.

The second season will see David and Max, after being dismissed from the GIGN – France’s elite counterterrorism and hostage rescue unit — find themselves at the center of an incident that raises suspicions within their unit and threatens its very existence.

“We’re starting filming on Season 2 of ‘Elite Force’ today. Audiences followed us throughout the first season, and it’s with great excitement that we’re embarking on a new storyline with everything dialed up: intrigue, emotion, action… Everything is in place to deliver!” said Leclercq.

Netflix has a track record with French action thrillers, notably “Under Paris,” directed by Xavier Gens, and “AKA,” starring Alban Lenoir and Eric Cantona.

“Elite Force” marks a return to familiar territory for Leclercq, who previously chronicled one of the GIGN’s most high-profile operations in his 2011 film “The Assault,” based on the 1994 hijacking of an Air France plane. He has since become a regular collaborator of Netflix, directing “The Wages of Fear,” a remake of Henri-Georges Clouzot’s 1953 classic, and co-creating “Ganglands,” a crime series inspired by his 2015 heist thriller “Braqueurs.” The latter ran for two seasons on the streamer.

Sisley, meanwhile, is best known for starring in the franchise “Largo Winch,” adapted from the Belgian comic book series, as well as the French crime procedural “Balthazar” which ran for five seasons on TF1.

智利驻印度贸易专员豪尔赫·洛约拉·卡斯特罗 (Jorge Loyola Castro) 在果阿举行的印度国际电影节上接受 Variety 采访时表示，印度和智利之间的视听合拍条约已进入谈判的最后阶段。

会谈可以追溯到 2025 年 4 月时任总统加布里埃尔·博里奇对印度进行的国事访问，这是自 2009 年米歇尔·巴切莱特访问以来智利总统的首次访问。卡斯特罗表示，这次访问启动了合拍片谈判。在访问期间发表的联合声明中，博里克和印度总理纳伦德拉·莫迪将视听联合制作列为两国希望合作的领域之一。何塞·安东尼奥·卡斯特继任者

“它已经开始，现在正处于最后阶段，所以我们希望能够尽快带来一些消息，”洛约拉告诉《综艺》杂志。

目前还没有确定的日期。洛约拉指出，这个过程去年才开始，并补充道：“我们真的非常希望明年我们能够宣布一些事情。如果事情发生得更早，那就太高兴了，但这也是智利的优先事项。”

An audiovisual co-production treaty between India and Chile has reached the last stage of negotiation, according to Jorge Loyola Castro, Chile’s trade commissioner to India, who spoke to Variety at the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

The talks trace back to then-President Gabriel Boric’s state visit to India in April 2025, the first by a Chilean president since Michelle Bachelet’s trip in 2009. Castro says the visit set the co-production negotiations in motion. In a joint statement issued during the trip, Boric and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi named audiovisual co-production among the areas where the two countries would look to work together. José Antonio Kast succeeded Boric as president in March.

“It has been started and now is at the final, final stage, so we hope that we can bring some news soon,” Loyola tells Variety.

There is no firm date yet. Loyola points out that the process only began last year, adding: “We really, really hope that by next year we can announce something. If something happens earlier, more than happy, but it’s a priority for Chile as well.”

The treaty is moving alongside a broader trade pact, the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. The two sides finalized its terms of reference during Boric’s visit and have held four rounds of talks since, the most recent in New Delhi in December 2025, according to India’s embassy in Santiago. India’s commerce secretary traveled to Chile in August to advance the negotiations. Bilateral trade grew from $3.84 billion in 2024 to $5.38 billion in 2025, with Indian imports of Chilean gold accounting for much of the rise.

Chilean producers are already lining up. Giancarlo Nasi, producer and CEO of Quijote Films, which operates out of Santiago and Los Angeles, came off a strong 2025. Quijote produced Diego Céspedes’ “The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo,” winner of the Un Certain Regard prize at Cannes, and co-produced Gabriel Mascaro’s Brazilian drama “The Blue Trail,” which took the Grand Jury Prize in Berlin.

“I love pushing the boundaries of what is possible and doing the craziest co-production that you can find. So co-producing with India would be ideal,” Nasi says.

Without a treaty, Quijote gets around the gap by bringing in a partner from a third country that has a treaty with Chile. A French company on Ukrainian drama “Pamfir,” which played Cannes in 2022, allowed Quijote to tap the Chilean-French treaty. A French company was also attached early on to John Trengove’s South African drama “The Smell of Apples,” which premiered at Toronto in September, and a French producer is on board the documentary Quijote is now making with Moroccan filmmaker Asmae El Moudir, who shared Cannes’ documentary prize for “The Mother of All Lies” in 2023.

A direct treaty would remove that detour. Nasi says the key is for Chile to build “a minoritarian co-production fund that is bigger and bigger and stronger so it can actually make a difference for an Indian production.”

A fan of Indian cinema since childhood, Nasi cites “RRR” and “The Lunchbox” as proof of its range. He has been receiving Indian projects, but has yet to find the right one. Many come from Indian filmmakers living in the U.S. who want to tell stories of migration and return, often on mid-sized budgets with no state funding available to them. He would like to make a film that spans India, the U.S. and Chile.
